Aucun corrigé officiel : réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level. Références bibliques, faits de la Sîra, positions de philosophes et de théologiens cités de mémoire et limités à ce qui est bien établi ; relecture par un spécialiste recommandée avant mise en vente. Neutralité observée envers les traditions chrétienne, musulmane et africaine. Les dates et récits de la période de Médine suivent les sources traditionnelles islamiques (« according to the traditional accounts »), discutées par les historiens.

questions.enonce_markdown:
“The hymns and prayers in the infancy narratives were characterised by joy and peace directed towards the birth and life of Jesus”. Comment

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Luke's first two chapters contain a series of songs and prayers: the blessing of Elizabeth (1:42-45), the Magnificat of Mary (1:46-55), the Benedictus of Zechariah (1:68-79), the song of the angels (2:14) and the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon (2:29-32). The statement is largely correct, because joy and peace run through them, but it needs one qualification: the peace they announce is bound up with God's justice and with a cost.

**1. Joy.** The theme is announced early: the angel tells Zechariah that the birth of John will bring "joy and gladness" (1:14). John leaps in his mother's womb (1:44), and Mary's spirit "rejoices in God my Saviour" (1:47). The angel brings the shepherds "good news of great joy for all the people" (2:10). These passages show that the birth of Jesus is received as the fulfilment of God's promise, and the reaction to it is praise.

**2. Peace.** Zechariah says that the coming of the Saviour will "guide our feet into the way of peace" (1:79). The angels proclaim "peace on earth among those whom he favours" (2:14), and Simeon, having seen the child, may depart "in peace" (2:29). Peace here means the wholeness and security given by God's salvation, not only the absence of war.

**3. Directed towards the birth and life of Jesus.** The hymns look both to the birth and to the future ministry of Jesus. Gabriel says that Jesus will receive the throne of David (1:32-33), the Benedictus speaks of "a mighty saviour" from the house of David (1:69), and Simeon speaks of a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel (2:32). The songs therefore interpret the whole life of Jesus, not only his birth.

**4. A necessary qualification.** The tone is not simply gentle. The Magnificat speaks of God scattering the proud, bringing down the powerful and sending the rich away empty (1:51-53), which announces a reversal of social order. Simeon warns Mary that the child is "destined for the falling and the rising of many" and that "a sword will pierce your own soul" (2:34-35). Joy and peace are real, but they come through judgment and opposition.

**5. Background.** The hymns echo Old Testament songs, in particular the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1-10), which suggests that Luke wanted to show the birth of Jesus as the continuation of God's saving work in Israel.

**Conclusion.** The statement is true as a summary of the mood of the hymns: they are full of joy and peace and they point to Jesus. It is incomplete if it leaves out the theme of justice and the warning of suffering, which prepare the reader for the rest of the Gospel.
